column2: Print it, or open the file in Excel or Google Sheets and use the Done / Owner / Notes columns.
Run it against three purchases you made last month — a small one, a big one and an urgent one. The urgent one is where the control breaks.
Anything you cannot evidence in writing is a gap, even if everyone remembers it going fine.

column4: Why it matters

column3: The indent names the project and the BOQ line or work item it is for.
column4: A purchase with no work attached to it cannot be reconciled later, and it is the easiest place for quantity to inflate.
column5: Does the indent form have a project and BOQ/item field, and is it filled?

column3: The quantity has a basis — drawing, BOQ, measurement or consumption rate.
column4: "Send 120 m" and "120 m per the BOQ line" look the same on paper and behave very differently at reconciliation.
column5: Ask the person who raised it how they arrived at the number.

column3: Existing stock and other sites were checked first.
column4: Two sites buying the same item in the same week at two rates is the most common avoidable loss in multi-site work.
column5: Stock register or system stock at the time of the indent.

column3: The required-by date is realistic and recorded.
column4: Fake urgency is how rate comparison gets skipped. If everything is urgent, nothing is.
column5: Compare required-by dates against actual delivery dates for last month.

column3: The specification is complete enough to quote against.
column4: Vendors quoting different specifications are not comparable, and the difference surfaces as a debit note later.
column5: Could a vendor quote from this line without phoning you?

column2: Getting a rate you can defend
column3: The vendor is on your approved list, with GST and bank details on record.
column4: Ad-hoc vendors are where compliance problems and fake invoices enter.
column5: Vendor master: GSTIN, PAN, bank account, date added, who added them.

column2: Getting a rate you can defend
column3: At least two comparable quotes above your agreed value threshold.
column4: One quote is a price, not a rate. The threshold is yours to set — what matters is that it exists and is followed.
column5: Written quotes against one specification, dated.

column2: Getting a rate you can defend
column3: The comparison is on landed cost, not headline rate.
column4: Freight, loading, GST treatment and payment terms routinely move the winner.
column5: Does the comparison sheet have columns for freight and terms?

column2: Getting a rate you can defend
column3: A rate contract is used where one exists.
column4: Rate contracts stop being useful the moment buyers forget they exist.
column5: List of live rate contracts, and whether the last five POs used them.

column2: Getting a rate you can defend
column3: The reason for not choosing the lowest rate is written down.
column4: There are good reasons — delivery, quality, credit. An unwritten reason looks identical to a kickback in an audit.
column5: A reason field on the comparison, not a verbal explanation.

column3: Approval limits are defined by value, and everyone knows their limit.
column4: Undefined limits mean either everything reaches the owner or nothing does.
column5: A written matrix: value band → approver. One page is enough.

column3: The approver sees the comparison, not just the final number.
column4: Approving a figure without its alternatives is a signature, not a decision.
column5: What is attached to the approval request.

column3: The approval is recorded with who, when and on what.
column4: This is the record that protects the approver as much as the company.
column5: Can you produce the approval for a purchase made six months ago in under a minute?

column3: Split purchases below the threshold are visible.
column4: Three POs of ₹49,000 against a ₹50,000 limit is the oldest trick in procurement.
column5: Same vendor, same item, same week — sort last quarter's POs and check.

column3: Goods are received against the PO, with quantity and condition recorded.
column4: Without a receipt record, the bill becomes the only evidence of what arrived.
column5: Receipt note with quantity received vs ordered, signed at site.

column3: Short supply, rejection and damage are recorded when they happen.
column4: Recorded three weeks later, it becomes an argument. Recorded on the day, it becomes a debit note.
column5: How many debit notes were raised last quarter, and how fast.

column3: The vendor bill is checked against the PO rate and the receipt quantity before payment.
column4: This single check catches rate creep, quantity inflation and duplicate billing.
column5: Who does the three-way check, and what happens when it fails.

column3: Advance payments are tracked to adjustment, not just to payment.
column4: An advance nobody recovered is a loss that never appears as one.
column5: Open advances by vendor, with age.
